facts.text: By 1917, Woodridge officially adopted its name and operated five Jewish‑owned cooperatives that helped Jews thrive amid the era’s anti‑Semitic climate.
Woodridge, once called Centreville, was a stop on the old New York, Ontario and Western Railway, linking it to regional trade.
During its heyday, Woodridge boasted dozens of summer hotels, bungalow colonies, and boarding houses, cementing its place in the Catskills Borscht Belt.
Ohave Shalom Synagogue in Woodridge earned a spot on the National Register of Historic Places in 2000, preserving its architectural heritage.
Silver Lake Dam, a historic waterworks structure in Woodridge, was also listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2000.
First incorporated in 1911, Woodridge began as an agricultural community with farms and boarding houses before becoming a resort hub.
